skript.thema: Claude's planned text watermark and what it means for pasted writing

teile.name: Hook
teile.text: Your pasted paragraph might wear an invisible fingerprint. Claude's planned watermark hides in the words themselves. But how?
teile.szene: Black-haired man in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses squints at a glowing page of text over his shoulder, painted urban open-world-game poster style, medium shot, neon night light.

teile.name: Crooked coin
teile.text: Imagine a crooked coin, tilted 51 to 49. At each word, the model leans slightly toward a secret green list.
teile.szene: A coin spinning in the air above a city rooftop table, one side lit green and the other red, painted open-world-game poster style, close-up, dusk light, calm space above and below.

teile.name: Red words remain
teile.text: Red words still show up, just slightly less often. No single word gives it away. Only the pattern does.
teile.szene: Close shot of a hand holding a magnifying glass over scattered paper scraps with blank lines, some tinted green and some red, painted bold-ink urban game style, warm street lamp glow.

teile.name: Who can detect it
teile.text: So can anyone spot your paragraph? Only a secret key holder, and short texts give no confident answer.
teile.szene: The cyan-glasses presenter in black leather jacket studies a long strip of text on a rooftop at night, shaking his head at a short snippet, painted game poster style, medium shot.

teile.name: Longer text, more confidence
teile.text: Long passages gain confidence, like more coin flips. Even text Claude merely edited could be flagged.
teile.szene: A writer at a cafe table flips a handful of coins in a long row, leaning in with focus, painted urban game poster style, medium shot, golden evening light.

teile.name: Practical takeaway
teile.text: So your short paragraph is just a few coin flips, too few to judge. Anthropic calls it imperceptible; one critic disagrees.
teile.szene: The cyan-glasses presenter in black leather jacket sits at a desk by a night window, thoughtful, hands paused over a keyboard, painted open-world-game poster style, medium shot, soft cyan glow.

teile.name: Call to action
teile.text: Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: The cyan-glasses presenter in black leather jacket smiles and gives a thumbs up on a neon-lit city street at night, painted urban game poster style, medium shot.

regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The user confirmed on 2026-10-05 that both new delivered videos are much better than before. Preserve the original painted world, recurring channel identity, matching main imagery, music and useful scene changes. The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Do not replace their actual AI scores or the existing 7/10 delivery threshold with the aspirational target.

skript.beschreibung: Anthropic plans to watermark Claude's text through word-choice patterns, according to a Daring Fireball column. This short explains the green-and-red word idea and why text length matters for detection.

belege.name: Anthropic's ‘watermark’ text adulteration in Claude is a perversion of writing
belege.text:
Discussed on Hacker News (825 points, 2026-08-16).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Daring Fireball: Anthropic’s ‘Watermark’ Text Adulteration in Claude Is a Perversion of Writing
WorkOS : Let agents sign up for your app without a browser.
Anthropic’s ‘Watermark’ Text Adulteration in Claude Is a Perversion of Writing
When I wrote this week about Anthropic’s announcement that all Claude models, worldwide, would soon begin “watermarking” everything they generate, including text, to comply with this EU regulation , we were left to speculate how this was going to work, because Anthropic offered not even a vague description of how it would work — despite the fact that the title of the announcement was, absurdly and insultingly, “ How Claude Marks AI-Generated Content ”.
My initial speculation was that maybe they’d hide invisible non-printing Unicode characters in the text. Just spitballing. Turns out that’s not what they’re going to do. What they’re going to do is apply a form of steganography, where the choice of words (or other token output) at inference time will leave fingerprints that can later, maybe, be detected probabilistically.
I initially guessed “invisible characters” not because I didn’t think of the semantic word-choice technique, but because I was a fool who took Anthropic at its word in their description of what they would do. Their original support document claims:
When a supported Claude model generates text, it weaves an
imperceptible watermark directly into the text itself. You won’t
see it, and it doesn’t change the meaning, quality, or readability
They say “imperceptible” and “doesn’t change the meaning, quality, or readability”. Their words. Not almost imperceptible. Not slightly changes the meaning, quality, or readability. That made sense to me, because that’s absolutely what I want — nay, demand — from any tools I use personally. It’s unacceptable for a tool to sacrifice an iota of clarity, coherence, meaning, quality, etc. for the purpose of embedding hidden clues within the text to suggest its provenance. That’s what I would and will demand. And Anthropic’s (original) support document unambiguously claims that’s what their system will enable. So if that were true, I couldn’t see what was left other than hiding invisible characters within the text.
My error was believing Anthropic that their system wouldn’t adulterate and corrupt the semantics of the text their models generate. That is in fact exactly what they plan to do. I should have my head examined for believing a single word of a document titled “How Claude Marks AI-Generated Content” that doesn’t explain, at all, how Claude marks (or will mark) AI-generated content.
How It’s Actually Going to Work
Yesterday, on an entirely different website than the original “How Claude marks AI-generated content” article (the one that didn’t explain anything at all about how it works), Anthropic published “ How Claude’s Text Watermark Works ”, which does actually explain in layman-accessible terms how it’s going to work. I will return to Anthropic’s new highly euphemistic and slightly misleading description below.
There’s a bunch of research on this topic, some of which I have also linked to below. But the very best description of the general idea behind the technique is an interactive essay by James Padolsey, “ How AI Text Watermarking Works” . It’s a wonderfully cogent read, and the interactive elements splendidly illustrate the main concepts. A+ work. If you have any interest in this at all, I dare say you must read — and play with — Padolsey’s piece.
But here’s my stab at a layman’s high-level summary. If you toss a coin N times and note the results, you can determine with a degree of certainty whether the coin is fair or biased. LLMs are, in their popular incarnations, non-deterministic. Ask the same question of the same model and you often get at least slightly different answers. Maybe the same meaning, but different phrasing. At each decision point for generating the next token, the model makes a choice. With these semantic watermarking techniques, they make different choices for some tokens based on word lists that could be called “green” and “red”. At each decision point, they’re a little more likely to pick a word from the green list than the red list. That doesn’t mean they never choose words from the red list. Just that they’re less likely to than they would if the adulterated marking technique weren’t in place. (Same way that a crooked 51-49 coin will still land “wrong” side up 49 times out of 100 on average.)
Words or word phrases are sorted into the green and red lists deterministically on the fly, at each “next token” generation point. So sometimes a specific word will be on the green list, and other times it will be on the red list. Someone with the secret key can determine which list a word will be on at each token generation point (which is how the watermarking is detected); those without the secret key cannot. This means there will never be a list of words that Claude prefers or eschews.
With coin flipping, the higher N is — the more times you flip — the more confident you can be that the coin is fair or biased. So too with this semantic watermarking. The more words in the text, the more accurate the analysis will be that the text was generated by a specific AI model or not. With too few coin flips, you can’t achieve any confidence at all regarding a coin’s fairness. With too few words (or tokens), there’s no way to achieve any confidence whether a string of text was AI-generated or not.
Given a string of text to examine for signs of a specific watermarking system, if there are more words tagged as green and fewer tagged as red than would otherwise be expected, the text can be flagged — with some degree of confidence — as having been generated, or merely modified, by the AI system that applies the specific secret-key watermarking system. belege.name: Anthropic trained Claude on illegally obtained Stanford professors' books
belege.text:
Discussed on Hacker News (597 points, 2026-10-27).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Anthropic illegally trained Claude with Stanford professors’ books
Anthropic illegally trained Claude with Stanford professors’ books
Anthropic illegally trained Claude on books from Stanford professors (Photo: JACK BERNARDO/The Stanford Daily)
Published Oct. 27, 2026, 2:46 a.m., last updated Oct. 27, 2026, 3:19 a.m.
AI giant Anthropic illegally scraped and pirated the work of over 10 Stanford professors to train its Claude models, a federal judge ruled in a May 2026 lawsuit.
Anthropic previously trained Claude on illegally obtained texts from professors Tobias Wolff, Abraham Verghese, Chang-Rae Lee, Daniel Mason, Hayagreeva Rao and Myra Strober. In Bartz v. Anthropic, which the Authors Alliance calls the largest copyright settlement involving an AI company, Judge William Alsup ruled that Anthropic could no longer pirate books to create a permanent central library.
While blocking the piracy of work to train AI, Alsup justified the legal acquisition of books to train Claude’s Large Language Models (LLMs) as fair use. He compared AI training to how humans can read, internalize and remember a book’s themes and style. “Like any reader aspiring to be a writer, Anthropic’s LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them — but to turn a hard corner and create something different,” he wrote.
The $1.5 billion settlement went to authors and publishers of nearly 500,000 registered works. Wolff and 27 other authors say the settlement isn’t enough.
“To put me to work that way, without remittance, is a form of slave labor,” said Wolff, professor emeritus of English and winner of the National Medal of Arts. “They’re using my work without paying for it. As time goes on, they’re going to make the lives of writers very difficult if there’s no fruit to their labor.”
10 of Wolff’s publications had been used for AI training without permission.
“[The settlement] still gives Anthropic pretty free rein to roam through our literature and basically take what they think will be useful and profitable for them,” Wolff said.
Wolff, along with English professor Chang-rae Lee, opted out of the Bartz settlement. In May 2026, they filed the separate non-class lawsuit Cruz v. Anthropic, seeking a jury trial for full statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, surpassing the approximate $3,000 of damages per work offered in the Bartz settlement.
Similar to the claims in Bartz, the plaintiffs allege that Anthropic illegally downloaded, reproduced and distributed their copyrighted books from “shadow libraries” like LibGen and PiLiMi, and that Anthropic broke the law by downloading and storing the pirated files in a central library.
“Our agents didn’t think the blanket lawsuit covered quite enough of the liability to us and are seeking redress in more particular ways,” Wolff said.
If Wolff and his fellow authors are successful, they would gain a permanent injunction against Claude model training using their works.
Paul Goldstein, a Stanford Law leading scholar in intellectual property and one of the plaintiffs represented in the class action, acknowledged the difficulty of addressing and preventing copyright issues for AI companies.
“The essential problem … is what economists call ‘transaction costs,’” Goldstein wrote in an email to The Daily. “Millions of individual copyrighted works may be copied in the course of any training incident, and it’s simply impracticable for the platform to obtain licenses from the copyright owner of every — or, indeed, any — single work.”
Outside of Bartz and Cruz, many authors, visual artists and news outlets, including The New York Times and Getty Images, have filed over 70 infringement lawsuits against AI companies. While Bartz established the current rule for pirating books, the legal future of mass scraping AI models used to train LLMs remains uncertain.
The Authors Guild is also pursuing other lawsuits, including one against OpenAI and Microsoft, as part of a “multi-pronged approach to ensure that the law is clear that AI companies must license the books they use,” according to The Authors Guild Chief Executive Officer Mary Rasenberger.
“Licensing allows authors and publishers to be compensated and to require the use of filters that ensure their works do not appear in outputs unless separately licensed,” Rasenberger wrote in an email to The Daily.
The Authors Guild is working with Congress to create national legislation that will require licensing.
“The Guild is up for the challenge,” Rasenberger wrote. “This is something we have been doing for 114 years, and the moment we are in today, while challenging, also presents opportunities for us to firmly realize our mission.”
For Wolff, this support is critical for the next generation of writers.
“I’m lucky that I’m able to have a life as a writer where I enjoy the profits of my work,” Wolff said. “I worry much more about the young writers I’ve worked with at Stanford and elsewhere being able to do that in the face of these technological challenges, because they’re very hard to grasp and to combat.”
Some authors are waging these difficult legal battles to achieve a sense of credit for their work, outside of the settlement payment.
“Attribution … is very important to the vast majority of authors, and not just academic authors,” Goldstein wrote. “The great majority of countries have something called the ‘moral right of attribution’ on the books to ensure that authors are credited for their work. The U.S., alone among industrialized nations, has no such moral right, which is a terribly unfortunate situation for authors generally.”
As Stanford authors and AI companies continue to navigate copyright challenges for training, both sides must navigate a “foreign land,” Wolff said, meeting at the intersection of creative rights and technological growth.
April Yu ('30) is a Columnist for Arts & Life (vol. 270) and a contributor to the News section of The Daily. She is an intended Human Biology and English major from N
